text:
Lynn Conway was a pioneering computer scientist and transgender rights activist. She made significant contributions to the field of VLSI (Very-Large-Scale Integration) design, co-authoring *Introduction to VLSI Systems* with Carver Mead and developing the MOSIS (Metal Oxide Semiconductor Implementation Service) infrastructure, which revolutionized chip design and enabled rapid prototyping. Her work laid the foundation for the modern semiconductor industry, and she was recognized with numerous awards, including the IEEE EAB Major Educational Innovation Award, the John Price Wetherill Medal, and induction into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2023.
A trailblazing figure in the computer industry, Conway faced significant professional challenges due to her gender identity. Fired from IBM in 1968 after disclosing her intention to transition, she later became a prominent advocate for transgender rights, working to protect and expand trans rights, promote gender identity awareness, and challenge the pathologization of transgender people in the psychiatric community. She was a critic of J. Michael Bailey's research and played a key role in the campaign against his book *The Man Who Would Be Queen* . Conway also contributed to transgender inclusion in professional organizations, notably helping to make the IEEE code of ethics fully LGBT-inclusive in 2014.
She was widely recognized for her activism, named one of the "Stonewall 40 trans heroes" in 2009 and included in *The Trans100* in 2015. In 2020, IBM publicly apologized for firing her and awarded her the Lifetime Achievement Award. Conway lived a life of resilience and innovation, marrying in 2002 and passing away in 2024 at the age of 86.
